Whether there is a decision inside the box changes nothing about what the output does to people, so the motion's mistake, if it is one, does not matter. Mill judged rules by their tendency to promote happiness. A rule of speech that bans the word decide would have no measurable effect on anyone's wellbeing, so there is no utilitarian reason to adopt it.

What matters morally is the effect of an action on welfare. A rejected loan application hurts the applicant in the same way whether we say the model decided or the bank's process produced an output. Arguing about the verb leaves every consequence where it was. A tenant evicted because a screening model scored her badly is equally homeless whether the newspaper says the model decided or the landlord did.

A Stoic will object that deciding is assent by a ruling faculty, so to call the output a decision is simply false, and false beliefs about what happens to us are the root of misjudgement. False beliefs matter when they lead to worse outcomes. Where the word helps people predict and correct the system, its looseness costs nothing, and where it misleads, the remedy is better oversight, not better metaphysics. The useful place to put responsibility is wherever it can make the outputs better, and that is with the people who can change the model.

A utilitarian should not care much about this motion. If the word decide helps people predict and control what the system does, using it is no mistake. The real risk is that people treat model outputs as unquestionable. That risk is reduced by testing, monitoring and appeal routes, all of which can be built whichever word we use. Effort spent on vocabulary is effort not spent on reducing harm.

Mill judged rules by their tendency to promote happiness. A rule of speech that bans the word decide would have no measurable effect on anyone's wellbeing, so there is no utilitarian reason to adopt it. Pilots say the autopilot decided to climb. The phrase helps them react quickly, and nobody is harmed by its philosophical looseness.

A Virtue Ethicist will object that calling the output a decision quietly moves responsibility off the people who trained and deployed the system, and that shift has consequences of its own. If the word really shifts responsibility, that is a consequence, and a utilitarian takes it seriously. The fix is to assign accountability explicitly in law and practice, which works far better than policing a verb. Call it deciding or not, the output reaches the same people with the same effects, and those effects are what need weighing.
